question: Are NYC streets more dangerous during nighttime hours? Present a chart and a conclusion suitable for a news report.

options.denominator: Two equal-length 12-hour clock-time windows over the data period; no traffic-exposure denominator
options.grouping: Daytime (6 a.m.–5:59 p.m.) vs nighttime (6 p.m.–5:59 a.m.)
options.reason: A reader may want to know whether the city records more crashes during the same number of daytime and nighttime hours.
options.answer: Across equal-length 12-hour windows, the file records 1,455,425 daytime crashes and 813,762 nighttime crashes, so reported crash counts are lower at night.
options.interpretation: This addresses whether the recorded crash burden is higher at night in equal-duration clock-time windows: the dataset has substantially more daytime crash records. Equal window lengths make totals comparable, but without traffic volume, trips, or distance traveled the chart does not establish which period is riskier for an individual road user.

options.metric: Percentage of crashes involving at least one person injured
options.denominator: All reported crashes in the same time period
options.grouping: Daytime (6 a.m.–5:59 p.m.) vs nighttime (6 p.m.–5:59 a.m.)
options.reason: A reader may define danger by the chance that a reported crash results in injury, rather than by crash volume.
options.answer: At night, 27.9% of reported crashes involved an injury, compared with 22.8% by day (about 23% higher).
options.interpretation: This answers how often a recorded crash involved injury, conditional on a crash being reported: nighttime crashes have a higher injury-crash share. Injury involvement per crash is a defensible severity measure, but it does not measure the chance of being injured per trip or account for differences in traffic exposure.

options.metric: Percentage of crashes involving at least one death
options.denominator: All reported crashes in the same time period
options.grouping: Daytime (6 a.m.–5:59 p.m.) vs nighttime (6 p.m.–5:59 a.m.)
options.reason: A reader may focus on the most severe outcome and compare the share of crashes that were fatal.
options.answer: Fatal crashes made up 0.245% of nighttime reports versus 0.101% of daytime reports, about 2.4 times the daytime share.
options.interpretation: This addresses whether a reported crash was more likely to involve at least one death: the fatal-crash share was markedly higher at night. Fatal outcome per crash is a defensible measure of crash severity, while the chart cannot tell whether a person traveling at night faces greater fatality risk because traffic exposure is unavailable.

answer:
- Across equal-length 12-hour windows, NYC recorded 1,455,425 daytime crashes versus 813,762 nighttime crashes, so reported crashes were less frequent at night ([chart](out/option_1.png)).
- At night, 27.9% of reported crashes involved an injury, compared with 22.8% during the day ([chart](out/option_2.png)).
- Fatal crashes accounted for 0.245% of nighttime reports versus 0.101% of daytime reports—about 2.4 times the daytime share ([chart](out/option_3.png)). These figures compare outcomes per reported crash, not risk per trip or mile.
